<reason>Side B (PRO) won a genuinely close philosophical fight. B's core dilemma — either consent means a bare yes (refuted by the pharmacy gouging case) or CON's enriched definition already concedes that conditions beyond agreement do the moral work — was pressed consistently from rebuttal 1 through the closing and never fully dissolved. A's countermove (packing fraud, voluntariness, and coercion into consent's definition) was executed skillfully, and the threat/offer distinction in rebuttal 2 was the sharpest single piece of philosophy in the debate. But B's landlord pressure question forced A to construct an entire baseline-entitlement theory of coercion mid-debate, which B's closing turned into the decisive observation: a "yes" that requires this much machinery to validate was never sufficient *alone*. A also swallowed the bullet that gouging a dying, fully informed parent is ethical, and B hammered that cost repeatedly while A's answer (upstream injustice, price-cap effects) stayed a policy argument rather than a moral verdict. A's closing claim that B "never rebutted" the exit-equals-voluntariness collapse overstated things, since B's whole strategy was to show the collapse itself proves the motion. Both sides answered pressure questions directly with proper A1/A2 labels; both had clipped turns as minor execution costs. B made the debate easier to decide and held the more natural reading of the motion's word "alone."</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's pressure question about the landlord truthfully demanding sexual favors from a tenant facing eviction he didn't cause. It directly stress-tested A's "seller didn't cause the desperation" screen, forced A to build new baseline-coercion theory on the fly in rebuttal 2, and let B's closing land the debate's most damaging line: "They haven't refuted the motion; they've recruited for it."</best_rebuttal>
